MUQATIL:18:9-10/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:9-10/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:9-10/r4.claim: The young men ask for mercy from God, which Muqatil glosses as provision from Him.

MUQATIL:18:9-10/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:9-10/r5.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:9-10/r5.claim: They ask God to prepare right guidance in their affair; rushd here means facilitation, and the wording involves fronting.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p173/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p173/r1.speaker: السدي
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p173/r1.claim: Al-Suddī interprets the mercy the youths ask for as provision and 'from You' as from God's presence.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p173/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p173/r2.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p173/r2.claim: The youths were believers who fled their unbelieving people, fearing they would be killed for their faith.

TUSTARI:18:10/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:18:10/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:18:10/r1.claim: The youths’ request for mercy means asking God to preserve them in remembrance of Him.

TAB-FULL:v15p161/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r1.claim: The youths took refuge in the mountain cave to flee their people while preserving their religion; they asked God for mercy from Him and guidance toward the right course.

TAB-FULL:v15p161/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r2.claim: Their request for a rightly directed course means that God make easy what pleases Him and their escape from disbelief and idol worship, and guide them to sound action.

TAB-FULL:v15p161/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r3.speaker: عمرو
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r3.claim: The youths followed Jesus, while their idolatrous king pressed them to worship idols; they refused and withdrew to a cave to protect their faith.

TAB-FULL:v15p161/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r4.speaker: عمرو
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r4.claim: One youth proposed his father's cave as refuge; the people sealed them inside, then a later Christian king removed the barrier, whereupon they awoke and estimated they had slept a day or part of one.

TAB-FULL:v15p164/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p164/r1.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v15p164/r1.claim: Ibn Ishaq relates that Christian belief had weakened amid sin and idolatrous rulers; Deqianus persecuted those who retained Jesus' religion, forcing the faithful to flee or face death and mutilation.

TAB-FULL:v15p164/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p164/r2.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v15p164/r2.claim: The young nobles sought God's help through prayer, fasting, charity, praise, and tears as persecution intensified; they were freeborn youths from prominent Roman families.

TAB-FULL:v15p164/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p164/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v15p164/r3.claim: Mujahid reports that at least one youth still showed a downy beard because he was so young.

TAB-FULL:v15p164/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p164/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v15p164/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says they were eight, naming Mكسلمينا as the eldest and the one who spoke to the king, followed by the other named youths.

TAB-FULL:v15p166/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p166/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p166/r1.claim: As Deqianus prepared a citywide sacrifice to idols, the youths prayed for the believers' deliverance; informers found them prostrate and reported their disobedience to the king.

TAB-FULL:v15p166/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p166/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p166/r2.claim: The king summoned the eight tearful, dust-covered youths and demanded that they sacrifice to his gods or be killed.

TAB-FULL:v15p168/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p168/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p168/r1.claim: Deqianus strips the youths of their rank and jewelry but postpones punishment, giving the young men time to reconsider their refusal.

TAB-FULL:v15p168/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p168/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p168/r2.claim: Fearing the king's return, each youth takes money from his father's house, gives some away, and sets out for a nearby mountain cave; their dog follows.

TAB-FULL:v15p168/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p168/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p168/r3.claim: They devote themselves to worship in the cave and entrust their provisions to Yemliha, who secretly enters town disguised as a poor man to buy food and learn news.

TAB-FULL:v15p168/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p168/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p168/r4.claim: When Deqianus returns to Ephesus and orders sacrifices, Yemliha reports that the youths have been found and are sought, alarming his companions.

TAB-FULL:v15p170/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p170/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p170/r1.claim: The youths prostrate themselves, pray for protection from persecution, and eat the small meal Yemliha brought as evening falls.

TAB-FULL:v15p170/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p170/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p170/r3.claim: Deqianus searches for the missing youths and tells the nobles he would have forgiven them if they repented, but the nobles urge him to question their parents and punish them.

TAB-FULL:v15p173/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p173/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p173/r1.claim: The two secret believers, Bedros and Ronas, record the youths' names, lineages, and story on lead tablets in a sealed copper chest by the cave, hoping future believers will find them.

TAB-FULL:v15p174/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p174/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
TAB-FULL:v15p174/r1.claim: They were richly dressed young princes who encountered one another while leaving a festival where their people carried idols; each had independently received faith from God and feared persecution.

TAB-FULL:v15p174/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p174/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
TAB-FULL:v15p174/r2.claim: The youths cautiously paired off to test one another's beliefs, discovered that all shared faith, and entered a nearby cave with their hunting dog, where God made them sleep for 309 years.

TAB-FULL:v15p174/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p174/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
TAB-FULL:v15p174/r3.claim: Their people searched for them but could not find the cave; they later recorded the youths' names and lineage, and a Muslim king succeeded the earlier ruler after generations passed.

TAB-FULL:v15p174/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p174/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p174/r4.claim: Another reported explanation says they fled a ruler's pursuit after one of them was accused of committing a crime.

TAB-FULL:v15p175/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p175/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v15p175/r1.claim: Wahb relates that a disciple of Jesus converted young nobles while working at a bath; after the king's son and a woman died there, the blamed disciple and youths fled with a farmer and dog, slept in a cave, and were sealed inside by the king.

ZAJJAJ:v3p270/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p270/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p270/r3.claim: Awaw means they went to the cave and made it their refuge; fitya is a collective plural like ghilma and sabiyaa, but the pattern is not productive.

ZAJJAJ:v3p270/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p270/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p270/r4.claim: They ask for mercy meaning forgiveness and provision, and for guidance toward what draws them near God.

ZAJJAJ:v3p270/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p270/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p270/r5.claim: Another vocalization of رشدا is possible, but رشدا suits the verse-ending pattern and means guidance toward what brings them near God.

NAHHAS:v2p448/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p448/r4.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p448/r4.claim: The youths took refuge in the cave while fleeing for their faith and asked for mercy to save them from the unbelievers.

NAHHAS:v2p448/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p448/r5.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p448/r5.claim: Rushd means guidance by which they could be saved; rushd is preferred over rashad here to match the verse endings.

SULAMI:v1p406#2/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r1.speaker: سهل
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r1.claim: The youths' request for mercy asks for remembrance and gratitude in every state, while asking for the easiest path of divine enabling.

SULAMI:v1p406#2/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r2.speaker: جعفر
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r2.claim: Seeing the youths from one's own perspective brings flight, but seeing them from the Real's perspective reveals unity and lordship within them.

SULAMI:v1p406#2/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r3.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r3.claim: A view of all created things from one's own position would turn one's sight away from the youths; the Prophet is both a beholder of God and beheld from Him.

SULAMI:v1p406#2/r4.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r4.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r4.claim: The youths were surrounded by lights of the Real, exaltation, and awe, explaining why the Prophet would flee if he saw them.

SULAMI:v1p406#2/r5.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r5.speaker: الحسين
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r5.claim: The Prophet would recoil from the overpowering spiritual states displayed in them, despite recognizing their lofty station of nearness and witnessing.

SULAMI:v1p406#2/r6.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r6.speaker: جعفر
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r6.claim: The awe of God's power, care, and guardianship over them would be unbearable; the flight would truly be from God, since what appears in them comes from Him.

SULAMI:v1p406#2/r7.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r7.speaker: جعفر
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r7.claim: One flees when looking from the human self but stands firm when looking from God; the Prophet's flight from unbelievers reflects the former human perspective.

SULAMI:v1p406#2/r8.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r8.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p406#2/r8.claim: Angelic lights are honors, while human lights are guidance, outward and inward; their greater awe explains the report that Satan fled from ʿUmar.

THALABI:v6p147/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p147/r1.speaker: ابن إسحاق
THALABI:v6p147/r1.claim: Ibn Ishaq narrates that pagan Roman ruler Decius persecuted Christians in Ephesus; eight noble youths kept monotheism, prayed and fasted, then fled the forced choice between idol worship and death after believers were tortured and displayed on the city walls.

THALABI:v6p147/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p147/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p147/r2.claim: The youths' prayer declares God alone as Lord of heaven and earth and says invoking another deity would be an outrageous falsehood; they ask for the persecution to be lifted.

THALABI:v6p157/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p157/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p157/r2.claim: The youths' taking refuge means going and joining the cave, a cavern in Mount Yanjalus called Khayram.

THALABI:v6p157/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p157/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p157/r3.claim: Their prayer asks God to ease for them what they seek of His good pleasure.

THALABI:v6p157/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p157/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p157/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets right guidance as a safe way out of the cave.

THALABI:v6p157/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p157/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p157/r5.claim: Another interpretation takes rushd to mean correctness.

THALABI:v6p204/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p204/r1.speaker: معاذ
THALABI:v6p204/r1.claim: The Prophet says reciting the beginning and end of Surat al-Kahf gives light from head to foot, while reciting all of it gives light from earth to heaven.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r11.speaker: الحسن
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r11.claim: One account says the youths fled to the cave to preserve their religion.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r12.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r12.claim: Another account says they were noble young men who met outside the city by chance; their eldest professed the Lord of heaven and earth, they agreed, then entered the cave and remained for three hundred years plus nine.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r13.speaker: ابن قتيبة
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r13.claim: Ibn Qutaybah says they were Roman youths who entered the cave before Jesus; God put them to sleep, Jesus disclosed their story, and they were raised in the interval between Jesus and Muhammad.

QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r1.claim: The youths were sheltered outwardly in a cave and inwardly under divine care; God took charge of them and brought spiritual states upon them while they were absent from themselves.

QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r2.claim: Their prayer disavows their own power and sincerely turns to God; He answers, relieves their need, and gives them a good refuge.

QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r3.claim: God effaced their self-awareness in the witnessing of unity and divine self-sufficiency, then returned them to sober discrimination after the state of union.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r1.claim: The opening idh cannot attach to the preceding question because the youths' flight was long before the Prophet; it attaches to an omitted command, remember when they fled.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r2.claim: The youths went to the cave and made it their shelter; Ibn Abbas says they fled there.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r3.claim: He glosses their going to the cave as fleeing to it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r4.claim: After fleeing those pursuing them, the youths prayed for mercy, understood here as forgiveness and provision.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p537/r5.claim: They ask for mercy from God alone so that it will make them independent of everyone else.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p538/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p538/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p538/r1.claim: Hayyiʾ means set right or prepare; rushd and its related forms are the opposite of error.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p538/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p538/r2.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p538/r2.claim: He explains the prayer as asking for guidance to what brings one near to God and pleases Him; Ibn Abbas says to direct their deeds toward God's love.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p538/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p538/r3.speaker: أهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p538/r3.claim: They parse the request as having an omitted noun, a thing of right guidance; further omission yields the sense, prepare what will enable us to attain guidance.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:10-12/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:10-12/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:10-12/r1.claim: The youths fled to the cave from their pursuers, devoted themselves to supplication, and asked for forgiveness, provision, and guidance toward what brings them near God.

JISHUMI:v6p4347/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4347/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4347/r2.claim: Awā means to return, and maʾwā is a place of return or refuge.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p145/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p145/r1.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p145/r1.claim: Ibn Isḥāq recounts that Christian society fell into grave error and idolatry under King Daqyānūs, who persecuted believers; eight elite youths fled, prayed for rescue, were captured, and refused the king's demand to worship idols, with Miksalmina speaking for them.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r1.claim: Awā means they went to the cave and made it their dwelling; the cave was in Mount Banjulus and was called Khayram.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r2.claim: The requested mercy means guidance in religion, or, by another view, provision.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r3.claim: Hayyiʾ means make easy; rushd is what seeks God's approval and what brings right guidance.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p155/r4.claim: He interprets rushd as a safe way out of the cave.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p659/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p659/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p659/r7.claim: The requested mercy is from God's stores: forgiveness, provision, and safety from enemies; preparing their affair means guiding them as they leave unbelievers or setting their whole affair right.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p498#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p498#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p498#2/r1.claim: Reports describe the youths as sons of nobles in the city of the unbelieving king Daqiyus, also called Daqliyus or Daqinus; they were Romans and followers of Jesus, though another view places them before Jesus.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p498#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p498#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p498#2/r2.claim: The youths' foreign names have weak transmission; al-Tabari's list gives Makselminya, Majseliniya, Tamlikha, Martus, Kashutunus, Birunus, Dinamus, and Yatūnus.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p498#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p498#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p498#2/r5.claim: One account says they hid their escape by playing with a polo mallet and ball as they moved toward the cave; another says they escaped while being taken to a festival.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r1.claim: People recorded the youths' names, fathers, rank, and disappearance on lead or copper tablets; some say two secretly believing judges hid them, either at their homes or in the king's construction over the cave.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r3.claim: The persecuting king is also said to have been a Roman ruler who sought to abolish the religion of Jesus and killed believers publicly.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r4.claim: The youths sought God's mercy, interpreted by commentators as provision, and a good way out of their situation; the author says this was a worldly prayer, while they trusted their afterlife outcome.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r5.claim: The majority read rashadan with both vowels open; Abu Raja reads rushdan with a rounded first vowel and silent second, while the majority reading better matches surrounding verse endings.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499#2/r6.claim: The words may also include mercy in the afterlife, and the author recommends this verse as a sufficient prayer for a believer's worldly needs.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r1.claim: A separate account says the youths saw their city's festival idolatry, believed, and left the people to avoid sharing their punishment.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r2.claim: Wahb's account has a disciple of Jesus work in a bathhouse, convert the city's noble youths, then flee with them after the prince and a prostitute died there and the disciple was blamed.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r3.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r3.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says the noble youths became believers one by one, met by chance beneath a tree, learned that their aims matched, and then fled together after confiding in pairs.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p499/r4.claim: Accounts say the dog belonged to a youth who hunted, or that a shepherd and his dog joined the group; its name is given as Himran or Qitmir.

TABRISI:18:10-12/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:10-12/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:10-12/r1.claim: The youths took refuge in the cave to escape their people and protect their religion, asking God for mercy, rescue, and a way to right guidance.

TABRISI:18:10-12/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:10-12/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:18:10-12/r2.claim: The prayer may ask God to provide a safe way out of the cave.

TABRISI:18:10-12/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:10-12/r3.speaker: قيل
TABRISI:18:10-12/r3.claim: Alternatively, they ask to be guided to a course that will save them, or for an arrangement that earns God’s approval.

TABRISI:18:10-12/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:10-12/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:10-12/r4.claim: The youths were believers who concealed Islam from a ruler named Daqiyānūs in Ephesus; he worshiped idols and killed opponents, though another account calls him a Magian who promoted that religion.

TABRISI:18:10-12/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:10-12/r5.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
TABRISI:18:10-12/r5.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr says the youths were close associates of the king who hid their faith from one another until they met, disclosed it, and fled to the cave.

TABRISI:18:10-12/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:10-12/r6.speaker: قيل
TABRISI:18:10-12/r6.claim: One account says they followed the religion of Jesus after the people of the Gospel had passed away; another places them before Jesus’s mission.

TABRISI:18:9-12/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:9-12/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:9-12/r3.claim: Awā means to return or take refuge; futiya is a collective plural for young men, like ṣabī/ṣibya and ghulām/ghilma, though such formations are not fully productive.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r1.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r1.claim: Al-Zajjaj says āwaw ilayhi means they went to the cave and made it their refuge.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r2.claim: Fitya is a plural of fatā, like ghulām/ghilma and ṣabī/ṣabiya; it is a collective form that does not generate parallel forms such as “ravens” or “wealthy men.”

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r3.claim: Some commentators understand fitya to mean young men; Ibn Qutayba says fatā can mean a fully grown man, as in the verse about believing women.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r4.claim: “From Your presence” means from You; raḥma means provision, and prepare our affair means set it right.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p108/r5.claim: Rushd means guidance toward what brings one near to God and is the opposite of error.

RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r10.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r10.claim: The youths’ taking refuge means they went to the cave and made it their dwelling.

RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r11.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r11.claim: Their prayer asks for mercy from God’s stores of grace, including guidance, knowledge, patience, provision, and safety from enemies.

RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r12.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r12.claim: “From Your presence” signals the greatness of the requested mercy, fitting God’s generosity and ample bounty.

RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r13.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r13.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r13.claim: Rashad can mean an affair endowed with right guidance so that they become guided, or that God make all their affair itself rightly guided.

RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p70/r9.claim: The temporal إذ cannot attach to the preceding question because the Prophet and the youths were separated by a long interval; an implicit اذكر, “recall,” is understood.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r1.claim: The dog was either their hunting dog or a shepherd's dog that followed the shepherd and youths; it was called Himran or Qitmir.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r2.claim: The youths' foreign names have weak transmission; al-Tabari lists Maksalmina as eldest spokesman and Yemlikha as the one sent with money, among six others.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r3.speaker: مقاتل
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r3.claim: The dog belonged to Maksalmina, the eldest youth and owner of sheep.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r4.claim: The story establishes fleeing with one's religion and leaving family, homeland, wealth, and friends to escape persecution; the Prophet and Companions did likewise.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r5.claim: Retreat to mountains, caves, or solitude is a prophetic and saintly practice and is especially favored by many scholars amid fitna and corruption.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r6.speaker: العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r6.claim: Seclusion can be practiced in mountains, at coasts and frontier posts, or at home; a report advises hiding and guarding one's tongue during fitna.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r7.speaker: طائفة من العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r7.claim: A group defines seclusion as inwardly and practically separating from evil while remaining among people.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r8.speaker: ابن المبارك
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#2/r8.claim: Ibn al-Mubarak defines seclusion as joining people when they remember God and remaining silent when they discuss other matters.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r1.speaker: النبي ﷺ
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r1.claim: A report says the believer who mixes with people and patiently bears harm is better than one who avoids people and does not bear their harm.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r10.claim: Any place away from people, including mosque retreat, coastal service, or home, fits the meaning of mountain solitude; mountains are named because they are common retreats.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r2.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r2.claim: A saying that al-Baghawi transmits as a mursal report from al-Hasan and others calls believers' homes their cloisters.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r3.speaker: النبي ﷺ
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r3.claim: In response to Uqba ibn Amir asking about salvation, the Prophet advises holding the tongue, staying home, and weeping over one's sin.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r4.speaker: النبي ﷺ
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r4.claim: A Bukhari report describes a time when a Muslim's best property will be sheep taken to mountain heights and rain-fed places to flee fitna for faith.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r5.speaker: الحسن بن واقد
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r5.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says that in year 180 AH celibacy, seclusion, and retreat to mountain tops become permitted for the community.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r6.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r6.claim: A long report says that in a corrupt age only flight from peak to peak or stone to stone preserves religion; family may ruin a person by demanding unaffordable provision.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r7.claim: People differ in capacity: mountain-cave retreat is the highest state, home seclusion suits others, and some can mix outwardly while remaining inwardly distinct.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r8.claim: Some veterans of Badr stayed inside their homes after Uthman's killing and did not leave again except for burial.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r9.speaker: وهب بن منبه
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#3/r9.claim: Wahb counsels a would-be recluse that people need one another, advising him to hear without listening, see without looking, and speak little.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r1.speaker: النبي ﷺ
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r1.claim: Uqba ibn Amir reports that God admires a shepherd on a mountain crag who calls and performs prayer from fear of Him, forgives him, and admits him to Paradise.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r2.claim: The youths fled their pursuers and turned to supplication; rahma here means forgiveness and provision, while rushd means success in right guidance.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets their request for right guidance as asking for a safe exit from the cave.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10#4/r4.claim: Another interpretation takes rushd to mean what is correct; similarly, the Prophet resorted to prayer when troubled.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r1.claim: One account makes the youths sons of nobles under the pagan king Daqyus, Romans who followed Jesus; another places them before Jesus.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r2.claim: Daqyanus, after Jesus, imposed idol worship in Ephesus or Tarsus; seven young secret worshippers fled with a shepherd and dog, and God blinded pursuers before they sealed the cave.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r3.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r3.claim: In another account, the youths learned faith from a disciple or earlier believers, rejected the king's idols, and answered his summons with words resembling 18:14–16.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r4.claim: A reported version says the king called them immature, delayed punishment, and sent them home to reconsider before a deadline; they resolved to flee while he was away.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r5.claim: One escape account has them playing polo and a ball toward their route to hide their departure; another says imprisoned youths slipped away while playing at a public feast.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r6.speaker: وهب بن منبه
QURTUBI-FULL:18:10/r6.claim: A disciple of Jesus worked in a bathhouse, converted local youths, then fled with them after the king's son and a prostitute died there and the group was blamed.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:10/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:10/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:10/r1.claim: The youths were Roman nobles whom Daqyanus tried to make idolaters; they refused and fled to the cave.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:10/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:10/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:10/r2.claim: Their request for mercy seeks forgiveness, provision, and protection from their enemy; they ask for right guidance in leaving the unbelievers or for all their affairs to be rightly ordered.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:10/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:10/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:10/r3.claim: The root of prepare means bringing a thing into a particular state or form.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p4#5/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p4#5/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p4#5/r1.claim: The prayer asks for mercy from God's stores, including forgiveness, provision, and safety from enemies.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p4#5/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p4#5/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p4#5/r2.claim: Their affair means their separation from the unbelievers; they ask God to prepare a right course so they become guided, or to make their whole affair rightly guided, or to ease the path to His pleasure.

QASHANI:18:10-11/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:10-11/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:10-11/r1.claim: The youths' cave is the body; they seek mercy from God's beautiful names, fitting their readiness, and guidance through descent to bodily existence for development.

QASHANI:18:10-11/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:10-11/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:10-11/r2.claim: By bodily attachment and tools they seek intellectual and practical perfection and a steady course toward God.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p134/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p134/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p134/r1.claim: Quraysh sent al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith and ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ to Jewish scholars, who proposed questions about the youths, a world-traveling man, and the spirit as a test of Muhammad’s prophethood.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p134/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p134/r2.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p134/r2.claim: A second report says the Jews judged that answering all three questions would disprove prophethood, while answering two and withholding the other would confirm it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p134/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p134/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p134/r4.claim: The sura’s opening connects to the prior sura’s affirmation of true revelation and humility: praise God for the upright warning Quran, which warns those asserting a son and promises believers reward.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r1.claim: Andalusian speakers commonly called Christians Rūm rather than Naṣārā; the youths ask God to grant guidance and steadiness after leaving their families’ religion for monotheism.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī glosses the prayer as making the whole affair rightly guided, like calling someone a lion.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r3.claim: Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, and al-Zuhrī read the forms of hayyiʾ with two yāʾs and no hamza, treating this as replacement of a quiescent hamza.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r4.speaker: الأعشى
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r4.claim: Ibn Khalawayh records al-Aʿshā’s reading from Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim without hamza; the form may reflect hamza replacement or disputed deletion, with replacement regular and deletion allowed in imperative or jussive forms.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r5.speaker: أبو رجاء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r5.claim: Abū Rajāʾ reads rushd with ḍamma on rāʾ and a quiescent shīn; the majority read rashadan with both vowels open.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r6.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the majority reading because it resembles the surrounding verse endings; he says the prayer concerns worldly need, while the youths already trusted their afterlife guidance, though mercy could also mean the hereafter.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143#2/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says every believer should use this sufficient prayer for worldly affairs.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r5.claim: The temporal idh is governed either by an implied udhkur or by ʿajaban; the youths made the cave a refuge and place of protection.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r6.speaker: المفسرون
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r6.claim: Exegetes gloss the requested mercy as provision.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r7.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r7.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the mercy includes forgiveness, provision, and safety from enemies.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r8.claim: Fitya is a broken plural of paucity, fitting their small number; Ibn al-Sarrāj instead calls it a collective noun, and the term indicates they were young.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p143/r9.claim: A report describes them as young Roman nobles, richly dressed with gold ornaments and sidelocks, following Jesus; another says they lived before Jesus.

SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r1.claim: إذ أوى may be governed by عجبا or by an implied اذكر.

SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r2.claim: Most read هيئ with hamza after doubled ياء; Abu Jaafar, Shayba, and al-Zuhri use two yā letters, substituting for hamza.

SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r3.claim: Asim's هي deletes hamza directly or replaces it, then treats the replacement as an original weak letter and deletes it; a poem illustrates weak-letter retention.

SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r4.speaker: أبو رجاء
SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r4.claim: Abu Raja reads رشدا with damma راء and silent شين.

SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:10/r5.claim: The common رشدا better matches the verse-end rhymes.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says he knows the Quran except the meanings of hannan, awwah, and raqim.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Ikrima, says he does not know whether raqim is a book or a building.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas also interprets raqim as a book; Sa'id ibn Jubayr says it was a stone tablet bearing the youths' story at the cave entrance, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd likewise says book, citing 83:9.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r4.claim: Ibn Kathir agrees with Ibn Jarir that raqim most likely means something written or inscribed, like the forms qatil and jarih.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r5.claim: The youths fled to a mountain cave to protect their faith from their people and asked God for mercy to shelter them and for a wise, righteous outcome.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r6.claim: Their prayer asks God to grant mercy, conceal them from their people, and arrange a sound outcome; a transmitted supplication asks that every divine decree end well.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r7.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p139/r7.claim: A report from Busr ibn Abi Artat says the Prophet prayed for good outcomes in every affair and protection from worldly disgrace and afterlife punishment.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r10.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r10.claim: They ask for exceptional divine mercy and a way toward deliverance and right guidance in both worlds; their request is granted beyond expectation.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r7.claim: The youths were few and inexperienced, yet youth makes people more receptive to truth and better guided than elders.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r8.claim: Their flight to the cave for their faith parallels Muhammad and Abu Bakr retreating to the cave of Thawr.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p448/r9.claim: Al-Harali distinguishes customary, extraordinary, and divinely bestowed orders of events; the youths ask for the highest, hidden kind of mercy.

BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r1.claim: The opening ‘when’ can function as an adverb modifying ‘wonder’ or as the object of ‘remember’; it means they went to and took refuge in the cave.

BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r2.claim: The youths were noble Romans who refused Daqyanus’s coercion to worship idols and fled to a cave in their mountain.

BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r3.claim: Fitya means vigorous young men and can metaphorically describe rulers even when old; a prophetic report prefers ‘my young man’ over ‘my slave,’ while Abu Yusuf says the term admits bondage.

BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r4.claim: ‘From Your presence’ means from the hidden treasuries of special mercy, inaccessible to hostile eyes; they ask mercy bringing forgiveness, provision, and safety from enemies.

BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p169#2/r5.claim: Both prepositional phrases attach to ‘prepare’; preparation means ordering their migration from unbelievers and perseverance in obedience, while rushd is the path to the goal.

BURSEVI:v5p170#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p170#3/r1.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v5p170#3/r1.claim: The cave youths fled Daqyanus, while seekers in retreat long for encounter with God; they seek rescue from the self and escape from existence’s darkness into divine beauty and majesty.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r1.claim: إذ may attach to عجبا or كانوا, or to an omitted اذكر; it cannot modify حسبت because the speaker's perception was not simultaneous with the youths' retreat.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r10.speaker: أبو رجاء
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r10.claim: Abu Rajaʾ reads رشدا with ḍamma on rāʾ and a still shīn; the meaning is the same as the common reading, which better fits the verse endings.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r11.speaker: ابن عطية
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r11.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the youths' prayer concerns worldly affairs because of its wording and urges believers to use this verse for worldly supplication; al-Alusi rejects the restriction and reads the prayer broadly for both worlds.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r12.claim: The fronted phrases emphasize the desired favor and make the petition's object of desire clear from the beginning; the construction may also be rhetorical extraction, meaning make all our affair right.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r2.claim: The فتية are the Companions of the Cave, taking the cave as their dwelling and refuge.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r3.speaker: الراغب وغيره
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r3.claim: The plural فتية denotes young, fresh youths; other authorities call it a collective noun, while most treat it as the plural of فتى by analogy with صبي and صبية.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r4.claim: They are said to have been young sons of Roman nobles and grandees, wearing gold collars and bracelets and having forelocks.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r5.claim: The explicit noun rather than a pronoun highlights their youthful state; another explanation is that cave ownership results from their retreat and should not be presupposed before it is stated.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r6.claim: The requested mercy may be great or of a particular kind; it is glossed as forgiveness, provision, and safety, while al-Alusi prefers a broad meaning encompassing these and more.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r7.claim: Their phrase من لدنك hints that the mercy is a gratuitous favor, not an obligation owed to them.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r8.claim: Their affair is fleeing the unbelievers while persisting in obedience; they ask God to arrange and facilitate it toward right guidance.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r9.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة والزهري
ALUSI-FULL:v15p210#2/r9.claim: They read هييء with two yāʾs and no hamza, replacing the hamza with yāʾ; al-Aʿsha from Abu Bakr from ʿAsim reads it without hamza, either by replacement or deletion.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r6.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r6.claim: The youths are spiritually the young people of gnosis, whose chivalry is to abandon all besides God and retreat into solitude with Him.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r7.claim: Their taste of communion spurs them to seek further ascent through the stations of spiritual bliss.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r1.claim: إذ is a temporal adverb attached to كانوا in verse 9, connecting the scene to the prior clause; alternatively an omitted “remember” makes it an explanatory restart.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r2.claim: The account is introduced in outline to show that the Cave youths' story is not God's most astonishing sign and that their protection was support for their faith.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r3.claim: أوى means to settle somewhere as one's dwelling; the place itself is a مأوى, as in Q 10:8.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r4.claim: فتية is a small-group plural for a fully grown youth and names the Cave companions; the explicit noun instead of a pronoun evokes their close ages and mature courage, sound judgment, steadfastness, and defense of truth.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r5.claim: The فاء shows that the youths hurried to pray as soon as they reached the cave.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r6.claim: They ask for comprehensive good in this world and the next, especially abundant divine mercy and guidance suited to their religious commitment.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p265/r7.claim: من لدنك conveys a special, abundant mercy directly associated with God, beyond the universal mercy all creatures receive; the youths seek protection from persecution, hardship in exile, and humiliation that could make them a temptation for unbelievers.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r1.claim: The youths ask God to arrange circumstances that secure steadfast faith and rescue them from the polytheists; preparation means furnishing the means to an outcome.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r2.claim: Their affair comprises faith and refuge from polytheists; God prepared protection from pursuit, the cave, bodily preservation, and long sleep, then made their steadfastness and revival a public sign.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r3.claim: With fatḥa on rāʾ, rushd means good, rightness, benefit, and soundness; with ḍamma it is synonymous but commonly concerns sound management of property.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r4.claim: This verse has only the fatḥa reading among the famous readings, while 2:256 and 4:6 have only the ḍamma reading.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r5.claim: The fatḥa reading here and at 18:24 suits the cadence; at 18:66 most readers use ḍamma to match nearby endings, while Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub use fatḥa.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r6.speaker: نافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو وأبو جعفر
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p266/r6.claim: At 18:66 these readers choose ḍamma for rushd to match the surrounding cadence; only Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub read it with fatḥa.

TABATABAI:18:26#2/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:26#2/r5.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:26#2/r5.claim: Al-Sadiq recounts that Quraysh sent three men to Jewish scholars in Najran for questions to test the Prophet, including the Cave youths, Moses’ companion, Dhul-Qarnayn, and the Hour.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r1.speaker: البيضاوي
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r1.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī says preparation originally means bringing a thing into a formed state.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r2.speaker: الراغب
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r2.claim: Al-Rāghib defines rushd as guidance to the desired end, the opposite of error, and says it is used like guidance.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r3.claim: Their appeal for mercy follows their helpless arrival; asking it from God specifically shows exhausted means and desperation.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r4.claim: The requested mercy may mean divine support, since no one else can support them; alternatively it may mean gifts reserved to God, especially guidance, as in the prayer of the firmly grounded.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r5.claim: Their affair is their perilous situation after fleeing persecutors who kill believers and force them to worship other than God; rushd means finding a path to safety.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#2/r6.claim: If mercy means divine support, the guidance clause explains it; if it means a specific gift, the clause adds a separate request.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r2.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r2.claim: The youths were believers under an idolatrous tyrant who killed dissenters; they feigned hunting to flee, and a shepherd’s dog joined after the shepherd accepted their faith.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#28/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#28/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#28/r3.claim: Reports make the youths princes, nobles, scholars, seven men including a shepherd, bathhouse workers according to Wahb ibn Munabbih, or ministers advising the king.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#28/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#28/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#28/r4.claim: Accounts differ on whether the ruler learned of their opposition before or after escape, whether they planned together or met by chance in the wilderness, and whether a shepherd or only his dog followed them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.claim: The cave story circulated in detailed reports from al-Qummī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Ibn Isḥāq, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, among others.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.claim: The transmitted accounts disagree even on major features, while reports about dates, rulers, lineage, appearance, names, and the title أصحاب الرقيم diverge still more.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.claim: One cause is the story’s prominence among People of the Book: Quraysh learned it from them, and its Christian images and monuments spread it widely, so communities reshaped it to fit their beliefs.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.claim: A second cause is Muslims’ broad collection of outside reports, especially through converts such as Wahb ibn Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār; later transmitters treated such material as prophetic reports.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.claim: The Qurʾān selects key lessons that serve guidance instead of supplying a complete historical account; it is a book of guidance, not history.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.claim: The Qurʾānic narrative first shows the youths’ truth-bearing withdrawal and long sleep, then their awakening and exchange that exposes them, and finally their discovery and the mosque built over them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.claim: The Qurʾān omits names, ancestry, birth, upbringing, occupations, social standing, dates, rulers, cities, persecutors, and the dog’s identity because guidance does not depend on them; historians and early exegetes filled these gaps, producing divergent accounts.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r4.claim: The narrative presents the youths sleeping in the cave with their dog for the stated long period, protected by the cave’s position and God’s care.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.speaker: أهل الرواية والتاريخ
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.claim: Most historians date the story between Jesus and Muḥammad; it is absent from the two Testaments, though some Muslim reports say Quraysh heard it from Jews, while Christians preserved it extensively.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.claim: Christian accounts resemble Ibn Isḥāq’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās in some respects but differ from Muslims on the number of sleepers, whether they had a dog, and the length of their sleep.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.claim: After centuries as a ruined, forgotten site, Jordanian excavation uncovered Rujayb; the author considers its archaeological signs and some Muslim reports the strongest fit for the Qurʾānic cave.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.claim: Amman stands on the site of Philadelphia, a major and beautiful city before Islam that remained under Roman control from the early second century until the Muslim conquest.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.claim: Other proposed locations include a cave on Mount Qāsiyūn near Damascus, one at Petra, a Scandinavian cave with seven uncorrupted Roman-looking bodies, and a cave near Nakhchivan.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.claim: No evidence identifies any proposed cave as the Qurʾānic one; the Scandinavian and Caucasus claims conflict with the story’s Roman setting and the limits of Roman power.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r3.claim: The three verses summarize their flight and prayer for rescue, their counted years of sleep, and their awakening to determine which faction counted the duration.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r4.claim: Each opening verse gives one of the story's three summary elements; later verses add what happened after the people discovered them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r5.claim: After leaving the people and their gods, they advise hiding in the cave, confident God will extend mercy and provide ease; these are the same gifts they requested on entering.

ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n8/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n8/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n8/r1.claim: Rushd means consciousness of what is right; the prayer introduces the Cave allegory and previews what verses 13 onward explain fully.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The verb rashada means to be guided and granted steadfastness; the expression about one’s affair means guidance in that matter.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The young believers' sense of truth made them disregard danger and expediency when the truth awakened in them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Their prayer for guidance and perseverance was wise and apt at this precarious moment.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: These verses summarize the whole story before its details, keeping its purpose in view so secondary details do not obscure it; the Qur'an often uses this narrative pattern.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Against exegetes who treat the promise of mercy and provision as the youths' own speech, Islahi says its certainty marks it as God's promise; a humble person could voice it only as prayer or yearning, as in verse 10.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r1.claim: The story in 18:9–26 illustrates the coming of the Hour and resurrection, making these ideas easier for people to grasp.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r10.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r10.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r10.claim: Meccans questioned the Prophet after learning of the story from Jewish scholars in Medina; the story answered their test, and verse 9’s question reflects the event’s astonishing nature.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r2.claim: Kahf means a large, wide mountain cave; Companions of the Cave names people said to have slept there for years and then awakened.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r7.claim: Although reports connect the youths to Jesus’ religion, the Quran does not identify them and presents only selected details for instruction; the author summarizes their flight, long sleep, awakening, and the townspeople’s recognition of resurrection.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r8.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r8.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r8.claim: The Quran gives neither the event’s place and date nor the youths’ number; guesses about their number are baseless speculation, known only to God.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r9.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r9.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:9/r9.claim: Long-sleep-and-awakening stories also occur in Indian scriptures, the Talmud’s accounts of people sleeping 70 or 60 years, and Christianity’s Seven Sleepers of Ephesus.

QIRAAT-ER:18:10:14#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:10:14#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:10:14#1/r1.claim: Replacing hamza with yāʾ changes the root from h-y-ʾ to h-w-y and may shift prepare toward make desirable or incline.

QIRAAT-ER:18:10:2#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:10:2#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:10:2#1/r1.claim: Eliding hamza after the dhāl of idh creates smooth liaison without semantic change.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r1.speaker: IK, Ṭs
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r1.claim: The youths, the Companions of the Cave, fled to God for the sake of their religion.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r10.speaker: R, Ṭs, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r10.claim: Their prayer sought guidance, knowledge, provision, patience, safety from enemies, and eventual deliverance.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r11.speaker: Prophet
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r11.claim: Their prayer is compared with a hadith prayer asking God to make the ends of all affairs virtuous.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r12.speaker: Ṭs
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r12.claim: Some say they asked God eventually to grant them a safe way out of the cave.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r13.speaker: Aj
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r13.claim: The cave is where they withdrew after despairing of the world’s kindness and sought God’s protection alone.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r14.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r14.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r14.claim: A mystical interpretation makes the cave a symbol of the heart.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r15.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r15.speaker: Th
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r15.claim: Some reports say the youths spent their cave years praying, praising God, and devoting themselves to Him.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r16.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r16.speaker: ST
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r16.claim: For some, asking for mercy meant asking God to preserve them through His remembrance.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r17.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r17.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r17.claim: Their prolonged life can symbolize remembrance that takes a person beyond ordinary time.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r2.speaker: Th, Ṭs
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r2.claim: They sought refuge from King Daqyānūs, also called Daqyūs in another report.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r3.speaker: Ṭs
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r3.claim: Daqyānūs may Arabize Decius, the king in the Christian account who tried to force idol worship.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r4.speaker: al-Ṭabrisī
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r4.claim: Al-Ṭabrisī also reports a possibility from some Christian sources that the persecuting king was Zoroastrian.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r5.speaker: Ṭs, Q
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r5.claim: Some accounts place the youths among the king’s courtiers; another says they were sons of local noble families.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r6.speaker: Th, Ṭs
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r6.claim: Some reports say the youths lived in Ephesus and hid their belief from fear of persecution.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r7.speaker: Th
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r7.claim: Others identify them as Christians preserving their faith and practices amid corruption, oppressive rule, and idolatry.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r8.speaker: Th
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r8.claim: After learning they were in a cave, the king sealed its entrance, expecting hunger and thirst to kill them.

STUDYQURAN:18:10/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r9.speaker: R, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:10/r9.claim: The mercy they requested from God’s Presence is explained as coming from His storehouse of Mercy.
